/--
Let $f(n)$ be an additive function (so that $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$
if $(a,b)=1$ such that $\limsup_{p,k} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n (f(n+1)−f(n))/ \log n = ∞$?

The answer is no; this follows from a construction of Wirsing [Wi81], rediscovered by
Archivara [Ar25] and formalised in Lean by Aristotle [ArWu25].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos897.lean"]
theorem erdos_897.parts.i : answer(False) ↔ ∀ (f : ℕ → ℝ),
    (∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b) →
    ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {(p, k) : ℕ × ℕ | p.Prime}).limsup
      (fun (p, k) => (f (p^k) / (p^k : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤) →
    Filter.atTop.limsup (fun (n : ℕ) => ((f (n+1) - f n) / (n : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/--

if $(a,b)=1$) such that $\limsup_{p,k} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n f(n+1)/ f(n) = ∞$?

The answer is no; the same counterexample is formalised in Lean by Aristotle [ArWu25].
-/

  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos897.lean"]

    ((Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {(p, k) : ℕ × ℕ | p.Prime}).limsup
      (fun (p, k) => (f (p^k) / (p^k : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤) →
    Filter.atTop.limsup (fun (n : ℕ) => (f (n+1) / f n : EReal)) = ⊤ := by
  sorry

/--
Wirsing [Wi70] proved that if $|f(n+1)−f(n)| ≤ C$ then $f(n) = c \log n + O(1)$ for some constant
$c$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_897.variants.log_growth
    (f : ℕ → ℝ)
    (hf : ∀ᵉ (a > 0) (b > 0), a.Coprime b → f (a * b) = f a + f b)
    (C : ℝ) (hf' : ∀ n, |f (n+1) - f n| ≤ C) :
    ∃ c, ∃ (O : ℕ → ℝ), O =O[Filter.atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ) ∧
      ∀ n, f n ≤ c*Real.log n + O n := by
  sorry


/--
Let $f(n)$ be an additive function (so that $f(ab)=f(a)+f(b)$
if $(a,b)=1$) such that $\limsup_{p,k} f(p^k) / \log(p^k) = ∞$ and $f(p^k) = f(p)$
or $f(p^k) = kf(p)$.
Is it true that $\limsup_n (f(n+1)−f(n))/ \log n = ∞$?

The known counterexample does not satisfy either of these extra hypotheses, so this variant remains
open.
-/

findings.description: The filter in lines 47–48 sends both p and k to infinity, rather than taking the limsup as the prime power q = p^k tends to infinity. This imposes a stronger growth hypothesis on the arbitrary additive function. For example, f(n) = ν₂(n)^2 log 2 is additive and satisfies f(2^k)/log(2^k) = k for k > 0, so its prime-power limsup is +∞. But f(p^k) = 0 for every prime p > 2, making the file's joint-filter limsup zero. These facts were proved in the scratch file. The cited counterexample satisfies the stronger hypothesis too, but that does not make the two growth assumptions equivalent.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/897 asks about unbounded normalized growth on prime powers. The cited Archivara paper, https://archivara.org/paper/df04f023-6ef0-4c52-bd12-18cdaa8f0741, §3, Lemma 1, explicitly says that q → ∞, 'for instance along q = 2^m as m → ∞', gives the required 'limsup over prime powers'.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a limsup indexed by prime-power values: `(Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {q : ℕ | IsPrimePow q}).limsup (fun q => (f q / (q : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤`. Equivalently, use the pullback of `atTop` along `(p,k) ↦ p^k`, restricted to prime p and positive k.

findings.description: The growth hypothesis in lines 63–64 uses the product-order `atTop` on ℕ × ℕ, requiring p and k to grow simultaneously. The source's prime-power growth also allows a fixed prime with unbounded exponent. The additive function f(n) = ν₂(n)^2 log 2 separates these assumptions: its normalized values on 2^k equal k, while its joint-filter limsup is zero because all prime-power values with p > 2 vanish. Thus this declaration changes the growth assumption, even though the linked counterexample happens to satisfy both versions.
findings.source_evidence: The second question at https://www.erdosproblems.com/897 uses the same prime-power hypothesis as the first. The cited Archivara paper, https://archivara.org/paper/df04f023-6ef0-4c52-bd12-18cdaa8f0741, §3, Lemma 1, explicitly allows the sequence q = 2^m to witness an infinite prime-power limsup.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the pair-indexed growth hypothesis with `(Filter.atTop ⊓ Filter.principal {q : ℕ | IsPrimePow q}).limsup (fun q => (f q / (q : ℝ).log : EReal)) = ⊤`, or an equivalent filter based on p^k tending to infinity.

findings.description: The conclusion uses `f n ≤ c * Real.log n + O n`, so it only gives an upper logarithmic bound. Although O is bounded in absolute value, this does not bound the error f(n) − c log n from below. The source asserts a bounded two-sided error. The conclusions are distinct even among additive functions: f(n) = −ν₂(n) satisfies the current upper-bound conclusion with c = 0 and O = 0, but is not c log n + O(1) for any c. This separation of the conclusions was proved in Lean; that example is not asserted to satisfy the bounded-increment hypothesis.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/897 states that Wirsing proved: if |f(n+1)−f(n)| ≤ C, then 'f(n)=c log n+O(1)'. The same conclusion appears at https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/491 and in Erdős, 'Extremal Problems in Number Theory' (1972), §VII, p. 85, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1972-05.pdf, as f(n)=c log n+g(n) with bounded |g(n)|.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace `≤` with `=`. Alternatively state `∃ c : ℝ, (fun n : ℕ => f n - c * Real.log n) =O[Filter.atTop] (1 : ℕ → ℝ)`. The equivalence of these two corrected formulations was proved in the scratch file.

findings.description: The strongly additive disjunct quantifies over k = 0. Additivity at a = b = 1 forces f(1) = 0, and the k = 0 identity then forces f(p) = 0 for every prime. The same disjunct consequently forces f(p^k) = 0 for every prime power, contradicting the infinite-limsup hypothesis. Thus the variant reduces to the completely additive case alone and omits the intended strongly additive case. A genuinely admissible omitted function is f(n) = ∑_{p∣n} p² for positive n, with f(0)=0: it satisfies strong additivity for positive exponents and the file's growth hypothesis, but neither current disjunct. All these assertions were checked in Lean.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/897 and Erdős (1972), §VII, p. 86, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1972-05.pdf, propose the two models f(p^k)=f(p) and f(p^k)=k f(p). These concern prime powers with positive exponent; the cited Archivara paper explicitly uses 'q=p^k with k≥1' in §2.1.
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict the strongly additive identity to positive exponents, for example `∀ (k p : ℕ), 0 < k → p.Prime → f (p^k) = f p`. Retain the disjunction with complete additivity. Restricting k to positive values in both alternatives would also be harmless.

findings.description: The first alternative includes `k = 0`, so it asserts f(1)=f(p) for every prime. Additivity already implies f(1)=0, hence every prime and prime-power value is zero under this alternative. Its growth limsup is therefore zero, not +∞. The strongly additive alternative is impossible under the preceding hypothesis, and the ratio variant only asks about completely additive functions. The scratch file proves this reduction and exhibits the omitted strongly additive function f(n)=∑_{p∣n} p², which satisfies the growth hypothesis but neither of the file's alternatives.
findings.source_evidence: The special models suggested at https://www.erdosproblems.com/897 and in Erdős (1972), p. 86, https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1972-05.pdf, are strong or complete additivity on prime powers. The exponent is positive, as also explicitly specified for prime powers in §2.1 of the cited Archivara paper.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `0 < k` to the strongly additive disjunct: `∀ (k p : ℕ), 0 < k → p.Prime → f (p^k) = f p`. The complete-additivity disjunct may keep k = 0, since its zero-exponent identity correctly agrees with f(1)=0.

reformulations.difference: Unlike the unrestricted declarations, using the joint (p,k)-filter for the infinite-limsup hypothesis is equivalent under either intended special additive model, with positive exponents. It is not an additional defect in this variant.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Put A(p)=f(p)/log p. For complete additivity the normalized prime-power value is A(p); for strong additivity it is A(p)/k when k≥1. In either case, an infinite limsup over prime powers is equivalent to A(p) being unbounded above over primes. Finitely many primes have bounded A-values, so this unboundedness persists after imposing any lower bound on p. For any lower bound K on k, choose k=max(K,1), and then choose a sufficiently large prime with A(p) exceeding the desired bound times k. This proves the joint-filter criterion, and the reverse implication follows from the same formulas. The separate k=0 error in the model identity remains a finding.

reformulations.difference: The joint (p,k)-filter for growth is equivalent to growth over prime-power values on the two intended special models, despite not being equivalent for arbitrary additive functions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k≥1, write A(p)=f(p)/log p. The normalized values are A(p) in the complete model and A(p)/k in the strong model. Both infinite-limsup criteria are equivalent to unbounded A(p) over primes: finite sets of primes cannot witness unboundedness, and an arbitrarily prescribed exponent lower bound can be met by fixing a positive k above it and choosing A(p) arbitrarily large. This equivalence does not repair the independently reported zero-exponent error.

reformulations.difference: Lean assigns zero to quotients with f(n)=0 instead of omitting indices where the ordinary real quotient is undefined.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For the specific claim that the limsup is +∞, zero-padding is equivalent to taking the limsup along `atTop ⊓ principal {n | f n ≠ 0}`. An arbitrarily large positive quotient cannot occur at a padded zero, and every quotient exceeding a threshold on the restricted domain also exceeds it on the full domain. A generic equivalence for all f was proved as `Review897.ratio_zero_padding_iff`.

reformulations.difference: The totalized Lean quotient pads zero-denominator indices with zero; the ordinary quotient can instead be considered only on its nonzero-denominator domain.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The +∞ limsup condition is unchanged by this padding: testing thresholds above max(B,0) automatically excludes zero denominators, while restricting the domain cannot introduce new large quotient values. `Review897.ratio_zero_padding_iff` proves the equivalence without any additivity or growth hypotheses.
